As the title says, if I plug in a power supply the mains goes into a transformer to step the voltage down and then into a bridge rectifier and it does not trip my breaker, but if I just plug in a long ass wire it will.

What is it about having it be coiled makes it not trip the breaker?

I've worked with more logic level voltage, but my current project will be run off mains voltage.
What is it about a electrical transformer that does not trip a breaker vs. a long wire?
Without a ton more info I can only guess but my best guess would be isolation. Your transformer is isolating the load.

Well I'm not really concerned with the load.

If a transformer is just two long wires wrapped around an iron core; what is it about the coiling that allows it to operate without tripping a breaker, but if I uncoiled the wire and plugged it back in it'd trip the breaker.

I think you're querying / discovering the difference between resistance and impedance.

If you put a rectifier in your plug to turn the AC into DC you'd trip the breaker with a transformer just as much as with the same length wire.

By wrapping the wire round anything we enable the magnetism given off by current flowing in one part of the wire to have an effect on other parts of the same wire, each turn of wire has an effect on its neighbors. This is called reactance. By using a ferrous core we enhance that effect even further. The reactance adds to the natural resistance of the wire to give impedence, which is basically alternating current's version of resistance. The higher the frequency of the AC the higher the impedence.

Also can I use a "common core", or does each coil need to be on it's own core?

Like if I used an iron rod, could I wrap the primary on the inside of the rod and the secondary on the outside? I've never seen this design used so i assume there is a reason for it.

Coiled wire provides an inductance to the circuit - putting the coil around a core and creating a transformer adds both self inductance and mutual inductance. These act as "resistances" to changes in current (caused by the AC source). When you just connect the long wire all you have is a very small resistance which will probably spike to trip your breaker. Just think of inductors as resisting changes in current. When your current is always changing they are always causing some "resistance". If your source was DC You would likely trip your breaker either way as the L would act like a short, without some clever circuitry. Not sure if this is what you were asking

Based on current evidence, what has been more damaging to companies financially? Fangames or spiritual successors?

Spiritual successors is a murky topic. The Bioshock series were spiritual successors to System Shock 2 specifically. They made enough bank to make a trilogy. Fallout New Vegas was a spiritual successor to the first Fallout games, and due to many considerations, was a driving force for them to eventually turn to kickstarter. However, the Fallout games were spiritual successors to the first Wasteland game. Cities Skylines was definitely a problem for SimCity. I would argue that Pillars of Eternity also was a problem for the Baldur's Gate "Enhanced" Edition.

Though part of me thinks you're really more asking about the current spat of fan games like AMR2 or how the Mother fan game spun off into its own property or Project M.

So from my casual perspective, spiritual successors have done more damage financially. But that's more due to the fact that when fangames start to take off, they tend to get hit with a DMCA, or come at a time when all they can do is boost interest in the original game(s), where they only help. But I am not sure how to classify the vanilla WoW topic. And if you put that under "fangame", it gets murky, because just because people are pirating a service doesn't mean they would have shelled out for the actual product (like HBO subscription vs Game of Thrones pirating). Best way to put it, either one is damaging, only when the fangame or spiritual successor is directly competing against an inferior product by the IP holders. But when they're not, they're the type of things that rack up interest.
